examples: Only when you are healthy can you enjoy life every day.
Technology has value only when it is used.
Only through effort do dreams become reality.
Only after becoming a parent do you truly appreciate your parents.
Only by actually meeting someone do you begin to see their character.
Only by failing do you gain lessons you can use next time.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to affirm a “necessary and sufficient” condition in terms of experience/practice.
Carries a nuance of emphasis and persuasion; suited to written language, speeches, and expert commentary.
Unnatural when used to ask permission, give commands, or make direct requests.
The subject is usually generic/unspecified; the following sentence is a general evaluation rather than a single event.

～てこそ expresses “only when one has actually done V does…”. Emphasizes the prerequisite condition for a value/understanding/ability to truly appear.
• Exclusive implication: if V has not happened, what follows cannot yet become reality/hold true in the full sense.
• The second clause is usually: ability (～できる), awareness (～わかる), evaluation of the essence (本当の～だ), discovery (～というものだ).
• Point in time: usually about the present/future; rarely used to refer to a specific past event.
• A nuance of honoring the “true value” that only reveals itself after real experience: 会ってこそ, 苦労してこそ, 失敗してこそ, 親になってこそ…
fields.notes:
• After ～てこそ, a specific simple past such as ～た is usually not used (though it can be used for a general truth/awareness one has come to realize: 失敗してこそ学びがあった is less natural).
• Does not combine with direct volition/commands: ×努力してこそ、頑張れ。
• The negative of this form is rare; to express a negative, use a different structure (～だけでは/～なしには…). meaning_vi: Precisely because… ⏐ explain: Means that precisely because there is A, B becomes possible. The following sentence usually has a meaning of possibility. ⏐ examples: 1. お互いに信頼してこそ、悩みも言える。
We can share our worries precisely because we trust each other.
2. 親になってこそ、親の苦労がわかる。
Only when you become a parent do you understand the hardships your parents went through.
mistakes: Used for a specific past event: ×昨日会ってこそ、分かった。→ 昨日会って、初めて分かった。
Confused with ～てはじめて: ～てこそ emphasizes value/prerequisite, not just “the first time”.
Used for direct requests/advice: unnatural.
JLPT N2: often tests the distinction from ～てはじめて, ～からこそ, ～あってこそ.

Emphasized reason; not necessarily an experience
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>するからこそ<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>する

Necessary condition for allowing an action

Used with nouns; similar honoring nuance

examples: I want to see him so badly I can't stand it.
I got bitten by a bug, and it itches unbearably.
I'm terribly worried about the results.
I'm dying to see this movie.
His rude attitude makes me unbearably angry.
The days go on, unbearable because we can't see each other.
fields.explain:
Strong nuance, an outburst of emotion; very natural with physical sensations.
Usable in both spoken and written language; also acceptable in formal written language.
Avoid using it with things that are fully controllable (×勉強してたまらない if you mean “I really like studying”; use 大好きだ instead).

Expresses an emotion/sensation so strong that it is “unbearable”, usually stronger than ～しょうがない, spontaneous and clearly personal.
• Often used with physical sensations: 痛い、かゆい、眠い… and strong emotions: 会いたい、悔しい、恥ずかしい。
• The preferred subject is the speaker; using it for others requires clear grounds (objective signs).
• The content is usually something that is emotionally/physically hard to control.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てならない.
→ ～てたまらない is usually more colloquial and expresses a strong emotion/desire one cannot bear.
2) Only used for subjective emotions/states.
→ Not used for objective facts.
3) In written/formal language, ～てならない is usually chosen. explain: Extremely ~ (cannot be held back) ⏐ examples: 1. 子どものことが心配でたまらない。
I'm so worried about my child.
2. 家族に会いたくてたまらない。
I miss my family so much.
mistakes: Wrong form: ×嬉しいでたまらない → 嬉しくてたまらない; ×静かなたまらない → 静かでたまらない.
Used for an objective fact instead of the subject's emotion/sensation → unnatural.
Mistaking it for the positive meaning “really like” can lead to using たまらない in the wrong place; consider 大好きだ/とても～.
JLPT N2: a trap distinguishing it from ～でしょうがない and ～でならない in strength and style.

rows: <ruby>退屈<rt>たいくつ</rt></ruby>で(は)しょうがない
Close to しょうがない
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>くて<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない

examples: I have a fever, but it's important work, so today I have to get to the office even if I have to crawl.
This is ramen I want to eat even if it means taking the train and going out of my way.
There is a proverb, “Take on hardship in your youth, even if you have to buy it,” and I think it's true.

A: Section chief, it looks like the trains have stopped.
B: It's an important meeting, so we have to get there even if we walk. Let's give up on the train and catch a taxi.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses strong volition: “will do it even if it means using extreme measures”.
fields.notes: Indicates forceful means. Followed by an expression of strong volition or desire, it expresses a firm resolve not to hesitate to use such extreme means in order to achieve something. （２５７）

examples: I'm terribly worried about tomorrow's exam.
I can't help feeling that he is hiding something.
I deeply regret this failure.
Her talent has a charm so captivating it seems almost a mystery.
I deeply regret that I couldn't help at that time.
I can't stop thinking about my hometown.
fields.explain:
Formal nuance, used in essays, academic interviews, and narratives.
Usually expresses lingering emotions or thoughts that won't go away.
Rarely used for direct physical sensations (pain, itching) — in that case たまらない is more natural.

Expresses an emotion/perception that “cannot be avoided, keeps going on and on”, with a formal, written-language nuance. Usually used for inner psychology: worry, regret, strangeness, lingering thoughts.
• Has an “irresistible” quality but is softer than たまらない; leans toward lingering thoughts/impressions.
• Common in phrases such as: 気になってならない, 心配でならない, 残念でならない, 不思議でならない, 悔やまれてならない, ～ように思えてならない.
• The subject is usually the speaker; it can be used for others in written descriptions of someone's psychology.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てたまらない.
→ ～てならない is more formal and often used in written language, but the meaning is similar: a strong emotion of “cannot help…”.
2) Usually used for strong emotions/worry/regret.
→ Not used for objective facts.
3) Does not emphasize intentional actions.
→ Mainly emotions that arise naturally. meaning_vi: Extremely, very, unbearably. ⏐ explain: Expresses a state in which some emotion or feeling arises naturally and you cannot control it. In most cases, it describes a state where you cannot hold back even if you try, so the degree of emotion is also very high. ⏐ examples: 1. 親友の結婚式に出席できないのが、残念でならない。
I'm so sorry that I can't attend my best friend's wedding.
2. 検査の結果が気になってならない。
I'm terribly anxious about the test results.
mistakes: Wrong form: Aい→くてならない; Aな/N→でならない; V→てならない.
Used for acute physical sensations (itching, pain) → less natural than ～たまらない.
Confusing the level of formality: ～でならない is more formal than ～でしょうがない.
JLPT N2: collocation traps such as 気になってならない／悔やまれてならない.

rows: ～でたまらない/～てたまらない
<ruby>退屈<rt>たいくつ</rt></ruby>で(は)しょうがない
Close to しょうがない, not archaic
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない

examples: We must obey the law. We must not discriminate.
Mobile phones must not be used during the exam.
Personal information must not be leaked to outside parties.
Alcoholic beverages must not be sold to minors.
The tragedies of history must not be repeated.
You must not enter the facility without the administrator's permission.
fields.explain:
Formal/written documents: rules, laws, ethical principles, official statements.
Rarely used in casual conversation; in everyday speech, ～てはいけない／ちゃいけない is used.
Often accompanied by adverbials that emphasize absoluteness: いかなる場合でも, たとえ～でも,決して.

• Absolute prohibition: “must not…”, legal/ethical/rule-based standards.
• Usually expresses general regulations, not aimed at a specific individual; the implied subject is “everyone”.
• Stronger than ～てはいけない (has the character of laws, charters, regulations, speeches).
fields.notes:
• Affirmative counterpart: ～ねばならない／～なければならない (must). Legal texts often contain both the affirmative and the negative.
• On signs and short texts, the subject and context can be omitted, leaving only the prohibition clause.
• 尊敬/謙譲 forms are rarely used; its normative character gives the sentence an impersonal nuance.
mistakes: Used for a casual personal reminder → sounds stiff/arrogant: use てはいけない instead.
Confused with べきではない: べきではない is advice; てはならない is prohibition.
Adding a subject, as in “私は～してはならない”, sounds forced in regulatory texts; the subject is usually omitted.
JLPT nuance trap: choose てはならない when “法律/規則/条約/倫理” are mentioned.

rows: <ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>してはならない。
ここで<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>てはいけない。
Admonition, morals; not an absolute prohibition
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>責<rt>せ</rt></ruby>めるべきではない。
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>破<rt>やぶ</rt></ruby>るものではない。

examples: The rain just keeps going, doesn't it? Since last week it's been raining and stopping, raining and stopping, over and over.
I'm writing a letter, but I keep writing and erasing, writing and erasing, so I can't get it done.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses the same action or state being repeated over and over.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: 行為(こうい)を（/状況(じょうきょう)が）繰(く)り返(かえ)している
Repeated actions
examples: 1. 雨が降ってはやみ、降ってはやみしている。
It rains and stops, rains and stops.
2. 書いては消し、書いては消しで、レポートがなかなか進まない。
I write and erase, write and erase, and the report just isn't making progress.
3. 冬休みは食べっては寝、食べっては寝（→食べっちゃ寝、食べっちゃ寝）で、３キロも太ってしまった。
Over winter break, I kept eating and sleeping, eating and sleeping, and ended up gaining a whole 3 kg.
4. （注）「～ては」一つだけで反復を表すこともある。
5. 彼女は毎年海外旅行に行っては、珍しい織物を買って帰ってくる。
Every year she travels abroad and comes back with rare textiles.
6. 留学のために貯金をしているのだが、なかなかたまらない。貯金通帳を見てはため息をつく毎日だ。
I'm saving money to study abroad, but it just won't build up. Every day I look at my bankbook and sigh.

examples: I wish my husband would help a little more with the housework.
I hope we become a society where people who work hard are properly recognized.
〈A mother's words〉 You're already a third-year in high school, so I wish you'd stop playing nothing but soccer and study at least a little.

A: Gas has been expensive ever since last year, hasn't it?
B: Yeah. I wish it would get a little cheaper.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression conveying the feeling “not expecting much, but still hoping”.

fields.meaning: To the extent of…, even going so far as to…
examples: I don't want to be famous badly enough to go as far as getting plastic surgery.
You shouldn't go so far as to borrow money to go on a trip.
He even went so far as to cry to beg for forgiveness.
I even stayed up all night to finish the paper.
Do you want to raise your evaluation so badly that you'd even lie?
She even used her connections to get the project approved.
fields.explain:
Usually goes with a negative judgment/dissuasion: ～てまで…ない／～てまでするな.
When praising someone's volition, add a positive context to avoid it being understood as criticism.
N + までして highlights extreme means (徹夜、借金、嘘、中傷…).

• Expresses an extreme degree: “going so far as to… (usually an undesirable/excessive method)”.
• An implication of criticism/disapproval is the default. For praise/strong volition, a clear context is needed.
• The agent is usually the same person for both action A and goal B.
fields.notes:
• Accompanying words often carry a negative nuance: 嘘、借金、徹夜、犠牲、中傷、違法、裏切り.
• In some emotional contexts the nuance can flip to admiration, but ambiguity should be avoided in academic writing.
• Position: Aてまで + main V. Do not use “BてまでA” when A is the goal; the focus easily becomes wrong.
mistakes: Confused with ～てでも: if the question praises volition → choose てでも; if it criticizes excess → choose てまで.
Used for ordinary (non-extreme) actions → unnatural.
Different subjects for A and B → the sentence becomes vague/nonstandard.
Tests often set traps with Nまでして vs Vてまで: look at whether what follows まで is して or まで to decide.

rows: Going so far as to do A
Focuses on a noun as the means
Even if it means doing A, still…
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>までして<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>る<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない。

fields.meaning: Will do it and show you
examples: No matter how hard it is, I'll definitely pass. Just watch.
I'll perform this magic trick for you once more.
I'll make her smile again, you'll see.
I demonstrated my symptoms for the doctor.
I was told no one could do it, but I proved them wrong and pulled it off.
How do you dance the samba? Please show me a little.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to affirm your ability/volition, or when actually “demonstrating something”.
Strong nuance; in formal situations it can be changed to みせます to be polite.
Usually directed at the listener as a declaration/challenge/encouragement.
Not used to ask permission/make suggestions. For the meaning “try”, use ～てみる.

• Meaning 1 (demonstration/proof): “do it and show”, an action that takes place right before one's eyes to prove one's ability.
• Meaning 2 (resolve/commitment): “will definitely … , you'll see”, a promise, vow, or challenge.
• The subject is usually the speaker; strong nuance, sometimes a bit boastful/proud.
• Different from ～てみる (try doing): ～てみせる is not “trying” but “doing it for sure, to prove it”.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てやる／～てあげる.
→ ～てみせる emphasizes “I'll do it and show you”, expressing volition/a display of resolve.
2) Usually carries a nuance of resolve or challenge.
→ Often used when you want to prove your ability.
3) Not the “try doing” pattern (～てみる).
→ An easy trap because of the shared “み”.
mistakes: Confused with ～てみる: choose ～てみせる when you mean “for sure/show you”, not “try”.
Used to ask someone else to do something: unnatural. ～てみせてください is the polite request.
Used for an action that cannot happen right before one's eyes (e.g., something in the distant future) with a concrete “show” nuance: use the resolve meaning, not demonstration.
In JLPT questions, the sentence comes with adverbs of resolve such as 必ず、絶対に, or a context of challenge.

rows: Do and show / Resolve to do
No emphasis on certainty; merely experimental.
Intend to do, attempt to do
Describes effort/intention, without the “show you” nuance.
<ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ず<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>する。

fields.meaning: It's not too much to ~ / it's all right even if ~
examples: Once your fever goes down, it's fine to take a bath.
It's no exaggeration to say that without him, this work would never have been created.
With this content, it's fine to broadcast it as it is.

A: Can't I drink anything the night before the test?
B: No, water or tea is fine to drink.
fields.explain: ◎ A formal expression meaning that it is not too much to affirm it.
fields.notes: Both 「…てもさしつかえない」 and 「…なくてもさしつかえない」 are used. A concessive expression meaning that the condition shown with 「…ても」 is fine and causes no problem. It is also said as 「さしつかえはない」. Close to 「てもいい」 and 「てもかまわない」, but it is normally used in more formal situations than these two. （２８１）

examples: He was said to be the most brilliant student since the school was founded.
Ever since I got a dog, a morning walk has become part of my daily routine.
This is the first time I've seen him since I graduated from university.
Since coming to Japan, I've been so busy that I haven't gone back home even once.
Ever since my child was born, I've made a point of not smoking in the house.
Since I started taking this medicine, my health has been getting better and better.
fields.explain: Expresses a state, habit, or event that has continued from a point in time in the past up to the present.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てから.
→ ～て以来 emphasizes a state/habit that lasts from a point in the past up to the present.
2) The second clause is usually a continuing state.
→ It does not just indicate chronological order.
3) Not used for events that have already ended.
→ If you are only describing a sequence, use ～てから.

examples: Having broken a promise, it's only natural to lose people's trust.
After practicing that much, it's only natural to win the championship.
It was a sudden parting, so it's only natural to feel sad.
It's only natural that illegal acts receive severe punishment.
There was a typhoon, so naturally the trains were late.
With an attitude like that, it's no wonder you get scolded by your boss.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a reasonable cause-and-effect relationship. Avoid overusing it in sensitive situations so as not to seem lacking in sympathy.
When praising/giving a positive evaluation: “して当然だ” = “deserves to”.
Compared with 当たり前だ, 当然だ is more formal and leans toward logical reasoning.

• An evaluation of something as “natural/obvious”, based on common sense, rules, or cause-and-effect relationships.
• Often carries a nuance of criticism when the subject suffers an unfavorable result: “deserves to be…”.
• When talking about natural emotions: “it's natural to be sad”, a degree of sympathy, no judgment.
fields.notes:
• Goes with verbs that have social consequences: 評価される／非難される／罰せられる／称賛される.
• Inverting the predicate with a noun: N + で当然だ (彼が優勝して当然だチーム＝sounds forced; it is better to split the sentence to make it natural).
• In essays, 当然だ helps wrap up an argument after sufficient grounds have been presented.
mistakes: Using 当然だ for someone else's emotions without context → sounds judgmental; consider using 無理はない.
Confusing the “should” relation (べき) with “consequence” (当然): if the question has a clear cause → choose 当然だ.
Wrong form: なA/N + で当然だ (do not use に/は).
The example sentence “勝って当然だチームだ” needs to be split: 勝って当然だ。強いチームだ。

rows: <ruby>批判<rt>ひはん</rt></ruby>されて<ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れたのは<ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ。
～のももっともだ／～も<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>はない
<ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>るのも<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>はない。
A normative recommendation, not a consequence
Colloquial, less formal than <ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ

fields.meaning: It is not necessarily the case that ~
fields.connection: V/A plain form + というものでもない / N・Na + (だ)
examples: Cheap isn't necessarily good. Of course, I look at the contents too.
Taking medicine won't necessarily cure you. Various lifestyle improvements are needed.
Being beautiful doesn't necessarily mean you'll be happy.
I'm glad prices are going down, but it's not as if anything getting cheaper is a good thing.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses the idea “one cannot say for certain that it is so”.

examples: Parents are always worried about their children.
Good fortune is something that runs away when you chase it.
Children imitate their parents.
Life doesn't go the way you want it to.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression that defines something, accompanied by a sense of exclamation.

examples: Here, bright colors such as yellow or orange would be better.
I'm good at sports that use a ball, such as soccer and baseball.
This summer, vivid colors such as blue and orange are in fashion.
Many students from Southeast Asia, such as Vietnam and Indonesia, live in this student dormitory.
To apply for this scholarship, documents such as an academic transcript and a professor's letter of recommendation are required.
Australia has many rare animals, such as koalas and kangaroos.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression giving concrete examples, meaning “such as ~” “what is called ~”.
fields.notes: Used to list examples. It implies that these are not all and that there are others as well.
